slides.title: Designing a New Clock Face
slides.storyContext: Zara is designing a clock face where hour markers are evenly spaced on a circle of radius 10 cm. There are 12 hour markers, so each is 30° apart (360°/12 = 30°). She needs to find the arc length between markers and the chord distance.

image.alt: Designing a New Clock Face — Circles

slides.title: Circle Definition and Basic Elements

points.label: Circle
points.text: Locus of all points at a fixed distance (radius r) from a center O.

points.label: Diameter
points.text: Longest chord, passing through center. d = 2r

points.label: Arc
points.text: Portion of circle's circumference

points.label: Chord
points.text: Line segment joining any two points on circle

slides.inSimpleWords: A circle is all points equally far from a center point.

image.alt: Circle Definition and Basic Elements — Circles

slides.title: Zara's First Clock Repair
slides.storyContext: An old customer brings a damaged vintage clock. The numbers are worn but equally spaced. Zara measures and realizes the clock face (radius 8 cm) has numerals at regular intervals. Master shows her: 'Each number is like a dot on a circle; equal spacing means equal central angles and equal arc lengths between them.'

image.alt: Zara's First Clock Repair — Circles

slides.title: Circumference and Arc Length

points.label: Circumference
points.text: C = 2πr or C = πd

points.label: Arc length
points.text: l = (θ/360°) × 2πr, where θ is central angle in degrees

slides.inSimpleWords: Arc length is proportional to the angle it subtends at center.

image.alt: Circumference and Arc Length — Circles

example.problem: In Zara's clock (r=8cm), what is the arc length between any two consecutive numerals (12 equal parts)?

image.alt: Arc Length Worked Example — Circles

points.label: Equal chords
points.text: Chords of equal length subtend equal angles at center

points.label: Perpendicular from center
points.text: Perpendicular from center bisects the chord

points.label: Example
points.text: Clock markers at 30° apart create equal chords in the circle

example.problem: In circle with r=5cm, find chord length for central angle 60°
example.solution: Using chord formula: chord = 2r sin(θ/2) = 2(5) sin(30°) = 10(1/2) = 5 cm

image.alt: Chord Properties — Circles

slides.title: Understanding Chord Distance
slides.storyContext: Vikram asks Zara: 'If we connect two clock numerals with a straight line, how long is that chord?' Master explains: 'A chord is shorter than its arc. The bigger the central angle, the longer both become—but the chord depends on the straight-line distance, using trigonometry.'

image.alt: Understanding Chord Distance — Circles

example.problem: For Zara's clock (r=10cm, numerals 30° apart), what is the straight-line chord distance between adjacent numerals?
example.solution: Chord = 2r sin(θ/2) = 2(10) sin(15°) ≈ 20 × 0.259 ≈ 5.18 cm (slightly less than arc length 5.24 cm)

image.alt: Chord Length in Clock Design — Circles

slides.title: Sector and Segment Area

points.label: Sector area
points.text: Area of 'pie slice' = (θ/360°) × πr²

points.label: Segment area
points.text: Area between chord and arc = Sector area - Triangle area

points.label: Clock example
points.text: Each hour section (30° sector) has area = (30/360) × π(10)² = 25π/3 ≈ 26.18 cm²

slides.inSimpleWords: Sector is like a pizza slice; segment is the curved part.

image.alt: Sector and Segment Area — Circles

slides.storyContext: Zara wants to paint each 'hour section' of the clock face (30° sector) with gold leaf. She needs to know the exact area to buy enough gold paint. points.label: Central angle
points.text: Angle at center; subtends one arc

points.label: Inscribed angle
points.text: Angle at circumference; equals half the central angle subtending same arc

points.label: Angle in semicircle
points.text: Angle subtended by diameter at circumference is 90°

slides.title: Finding Hidden Angles
slides.storyContext: Vikram brings a broken clock where two numerals are damaged. He measures the angle they form from the center (central angle) as 60°. He then wonders: 'If someone looks at these two numerals from the rim of the clock (circumference), what angle do they see?' Master smiles: 'That's the inscribed angle—always half the central angle. So they'd see 30°.'

image.alt: Finding Hidden Angles — Circles

image.alt: Inscribed Angle Worked Example — Circles

points.label: Tangent
points.text: Line touching circle at exactly one point, perpendicular to radius at that point

points.label: Two tangents
points.text: From external point, two tangents have equal length

points.text: Clock handle at edge is tangent to the circle

image.alt: Tangent to a Circle — Circles

slides.title: Measuring the Clock Hands
slides.storyContext: Zara is fitting new hands to the clock. The hour hand is tangent to a smaller inner circle (radius 4 cm) at its base. She realizes: 'The hand touches the circle at exactly one point and forms a right angle with the radius. That's a tangent!' She needs to find the length of a tangent from an external point.

image.alt: Measuring the Clock Hands — Circles

example.problem: From a point 10 cm away from circle center (r=6cm), draw a tangent. What is the tangent length?
example.solution: Using Pythagorean theorem: tangent² + radius² = distance². tangent² = 10² - 6² = 100 - 36 = 64. Tangent = 8 cm

image.alt: Tangent Length Worked Example — Circles

example.problem: A point P lies on a semicircle with diameter AB=10cm. If you measure angle APB, what will it always equal?
example.solution: Angle APB = 90° (Thales' theorem). Any angle inscribed in a semicircle is always a right angle, regardless of where P is on the arc.

image.alt: Angle in Semicircle Problem — Circles

example.problem: Zara's clock: r=10cm, 12 hour markers. (1) Circumference? (2) Arc between adjacent markers? (3) Chord length between adjacent markers? (4) Area of each sector?

image.alt: Complete Clock Face Calculation — Circles

example.problem: Two circles of radius 5cm each have centers 6cm apart. Find the length of their common chord.
example.solution: Using Pythagorean theorem: If d=6, r=5, then half-chord length h: 5² = 3² + h² → h² = 16 → h = 4. Common chord = 8cm.

image.alt: Two-Circles Problem — Circles

example.problem: In a circle of radius 10cm, two chords are 8cm and 8cm respectively. What can you conclude about the angles they subtend at the center?
example.solution: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the center. Both chords subtend the same central angle θ where chord = 2r sin(θ/2) = 8, so sin(θ/2) = 0.4, giving θ ≈ 47.16° for each.

image.alt: Equal Chords Problem — Circles

slides.title: Tangent From External Point
slides.storyContext: A customer brings a broken clock with two hands that were bent. Zara needs to fit new hands that act as tangents to an inner decorative ring. She measures: the hand attachment point is 15cm from the ring's center, and the ring has radius 9cm. She needs to find the tangent length to ensure proper clearance.

image.alt: Tangent From External Point — Circles

example.problem: From external point P, distance 13cm from center of circle (r=5cm), draw two tangents. What is the tangent length?
example.solution: Using Pythagorean theorem: tangent² + radius² = distance². tangent² = 13² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144. Tangent = 12 cm. Both tangents from P have equal length 12 cm.

image.alt: Two Tangents From External Point — Circles

slides.title: Zara's Final Masterpiece
slides.storyContext: Zara completes an antique clock restoration. The design uses overlapping circular patterns, where two decorative circles (each r=5cm) intersect with centers 6cm apart. She calculates the common chord to ensure proper fitting. Her work is so precise that customers line up to commission new designs.

slides.title: Circular Garden Design
slides.storyContext: Deepak is designing a circular flower garden with radius 5 meters in Deepak's backyard. He wants to calculate: (1) total area of the garden, (2) area of a quarter-circle flower section, (3) area of a pathway around it. His daughter asks: how much soil do we need for the flowers?

image.alt: Circular Garden Design — Areas Related to Circles

slides.title: Area of Circle

points.label: Formula
points.text: A = πr² (where r is radius)

points.label: Using diameter
points.text: A = π(d/2)² = πd²/4

points.label: Example
points.text: Garden with r=5m: A = π(25) = 25π ≈ 78.54 m²

slides.inSimpleWords: Circle area equals π times radius squared.

image.alt: Area of Circle — Areas Related to Circles

slides.title: Calculating Soil Needs
slides.storyContext: Deepak measures his circular garden (5m radius) and realizes he needs to order soil in cubic meters. His supplier asks for the base area in square meters. He calculates: '5 meters radius means 25π square meters of area. At ₹200 per square meter for premium soil, the cost is 25π × 200 = 5000π rupees. That's about ₹15,700!'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Sector is a 'pie slice' of the circle from center

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area of sector = (θ/360°) × πr², where θ is central angle in degrees

points.label: Example
points.text: Quarter-circle (90°) in garden: A = (90/360) × 25π = 25π/4 ≈ 19.63 m²

example.problem: Sector with r=6cm and central angle 120°. Find area.

slides.title: Designing Flower Sections
slides.storyContext: Neha suggests dividing the circular garden into 4 equal sections (quarter circles, 90° each) for different flowers: roses (north), tulips (east), marigolds (south), sunflowers (west). Each quarter has area 25π/4 ≈ 19.63 m². Deepak realizes: 'Four quarters of the same size make one full circle—that's 4 × 19.63 ≈ 78.54 m², which matches our total!'

image.alt: Designing Flower Sections — Areas Related to Circles

example.problem: One quarter-circle section of Deepak's garden (r=5m, θ=90°). What is the area?

image.alt: Sector Area Worked Example — Areas Related to Circles

slides.title: Area of Segment

points.label: Definition
points.text: Segment is region between chord and arc (curved part without the triangle)

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area of segment = Area of sector - Area of triangle

points.label: Example
points.text: If sector angle = 60°: Area of triangle = (1/2)r²sin(60°) = (1/2)(25)(√3/2) = 25√3/4. Segment = (60/360)×25π - 25√3/4

slides.inSimpleWords: Segment area = pie slice area minus the triangle inside it.

image.alt: Area of Segment — Areas Related to Circles

slides.title: Curved Pathways
slides.storyContext: Deepak wants to add a curved stone pathway along the edge of the rose section. The pathway curves along the arc but doesn't fill the entire sector—it's only the region between the chord (straight line) and the curved arc. This is a segment. He needs to calculate how many stones are needed to cover the segment area.

image.alt: Curved Pathways — Areas Related to Circles

example.problem: Circle r=7cm, chord at central angle 90°. Find segment area.
example.solution: Sector area = (90/360) × π(49) = 49π/4. Triangle (right angle at center) area = (1/2)(7)(7) = 49/2. Segment area = 49π/4 - 49/2 = 49(π/4 - 1/2) ≈ 9.76 cm²

image.alt: Segment Calculation Detailed — Areas Related to Circles

slides.title: Area of Ring (Annulus)

points.label: Definition
points.text: Area between two concentric circles

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area = π(R² - r²), where R is outer radius, r is inner radius

points.label: Example
points.text: Pathway around garden: outer radius 6m, inner 5m. Area = π(36 - 25) = 11π ≈ 34.56 m²

slides.inSimpleWords: Ring area = big circle minus small circle inside.

image.alt: Area of Ring (Annulus) — Areas Related to Circles

slides.title: Adding the Grass Border
slides.storyContext: Mom suggests adding a grass border (walkway) around the entire flower garden. It's 1 meter wide. So the outer circle has radius 6m (5m garden + 1m border). The grass area is the difference between these two circles. Deepak calculates: 'The ring area is π(6² - 5²) = π(36 - 25) = 11π ≈ 34.56 m². That's how much grass seed I need!'

image.alt: Adding the Grass Border — Areas Related to Circles

example.problem: Deepak's pathway ring: inner circle r=5m, outer circle r=6m. What is the grass area?

example.problem: Garden design: Circle r=5m (flowers), surrounding pathway (ring) with outer r=6m (grass), and one quarter-sector (90°) for vegetables. Calculate: (1) Flower area, (2) Grass pathway area, (3) Vegetable sector area, (4) Total area. Cost: ₹100/m² for flowers, ₹50/m² for grass, ₹75/m² for vegetables.

image.alt: Deepak's Complete Garden Cost Calculation — Areas Related to Circles

example.problem: Two equal circles r=4cm intersect. Distance between centers = 4cm. Find total area of union (covered region).
example.solution: Each circle contributes a segment. Using chord at distance 2 from center: segment angle = 120° per circle. Area = 2 × [Sector(120°) - Triangle] = 2 × [16π/3 - 4√3] = 32π/3 - 8√3 ≈ 20.15cm²

image.alt: Complex Overlap Problem — Areas Related to Circles

example.problem: Two neighbors have circular gardens (r=5m each, centers 4m apart). They want to fence the area covered by at least one garden. Calculate the union area.
example.solution: Each circle: A = 25π. Intersection: 2 segments with chord at distance 2m. Each segment ≈ 8.33m². Union = 25π + 25π - 2(8.33) ≈ 157.08 - 16.66 ≈ 140.42 m²

image.alt: Two-Garden Intersection — Areas Related to Circles

example.problem: In Deepak's garden (r=5m), if he wants three sectors with central angles in ratio 2:3:4, what are the areas of each sector?

image.alt: Sector Proportionality Problem — Areas Related to Circles

slides.title: Segment Problem: Half-Circle Case
slides.storyContext: Neha designs a semicircular flower bed with radius 4m. She wants to create a walking path that follows the inner chord (diameter) level. The segment area above this path will have decorative flowers. She calculates: Semicircle area = 25π/2 ≈ 39.27 m². The 'segment' between the diameter and the arc is just the semicircle itself.

image.alt: Segment Problem: Half-Circle Case — Areas Related to Circles

example.problem: In circle r=6cm with central angle 60°, find the segment area between the chord and arc.

image.alt: Segment Area for 60° Angle — Areas Related to Circles

example.problem: Deepak compares two border designs: (1) Full ring r_inner=5m, r_outer=6m, (2) Half-ring (semicircular border) same radii. Both cost ₹1000/m². What is the cost difference?
example.solution: Full ring area = 11π ≈ 34.56 m², cost = ₹34,560. Half-ring area = 11π/2 ≈ 17.28 m², cost = ₹17,280. Difference = ₹17,280

image.alt: Ring Cost Comparison — Areas Related to Circles

example.problem: Cylindrical container r=5cm, h=20cm. Cost of plastic: ₹0.50 per cm². She needs 1000 containers. (1) Volume per container? (2) TSA per container? (3) Total plastic needed? (4) Total cost?

example.problem: A toy is made of hemisphere (r=3cm) joined to cone (r=3cm, h=4cm). Find total surface area.
example.solution: Hemisphere CSA = 2π(9) = 18π. Cone slant height l = √(9+16) = 5. Cone CSA = π(3)(5) = 15π. Total = 18π + 15π = 33π ≈ 103.67 cm²

image.alt: Hemisphere and Cone Combination — Surface Areas and Volumes

example.problem: A cylinder has radius 4cm and height 8cm. If radius is doubled but height is halved, how does volume change?
example.solution: Original V = π(16)(8) = 128π. New V = π(64)(4) = 256π. Change = 256π/128π = 2 times (volume doubles).

image.alt: Volume Change Problem — Surface Areas and Volumes

example.problem: Nisha can make 1000 cylinders (r=5, h=20) at ₹0.50/cm² plastic + ₹5000 setup cost = ₹8854.50 total. Or 500 larger cylinders (r=6, h=25) at same rate + ₹3000 setup = ₹7500 total. Which is cheaper per unit, and what's the volume ratio?
example.solution: Small: ₹8.85/unit, V=1570.8 cm³. Large: ₹15/unit, V≈2827 cm³. Small is cheaper per unit, but large has more volume per container. Choose based on product needs.

image.alt: Cost Optimization Problem — Surface Areas and Volumes

example.problem: If a container has dimensions scaled by factor k, how do volume and surface area change? If k=2, compare new and old.
example.solution: New volume = k³ × old = 8 × old. New SA = k² × old = 4 × old. Volume increases more dramatically than surface area when scaling up.

slides.title: Comparing Container Efficiency
slides.storyContext: Nisha realizes that different shapes can hold similar volumes but use different amounts of material. A sphere is theoretically the most efficient (smallest surface area for given volume). She compares: a cylinder (r=5, h=20) vs. a sphere (r=6.5). Both have roughly V ≈ 1500 cm³, but sphere uses much less material.

image.alt: Comparing Container Efficiency — Surface Areas and Volumes

example.problem: Compare material usage: Cylinder (r=5, h=20) vs Sphere (r=6.5). Which uses less material for similar volume?
example.solution: Cylinder: V ≈ 1571 cm³, TSA ≈ 785 cm². Sphere: V ≈ 1150 cm³, SA ≈ 531 cm². Sphere uses ~32% less material for comparable volume, making it more economical.
